prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid

outputs.L1:
At the stables, each stall bore a name. Biscuit stood aloof — I faced, always and invariably, his clockwork tail. Crab knew the salt lick too intimately. Trapezoid had mastered stillness: a midnight mare, sternest and tallest of them all, her chest pressed against the edges of her stall. I was not afraid of Never, the chestnut gelding, and so I rode his iron haunches as far as Panther Gap. Never and I lived in Virginia then. We could neither flee nor be kept. Seldom did I reach the little mountain without him, its easy crests turning valleys into fields of indifferent grass.

What was that low sound I heard, alone with Never? A lone horse, a lodestar, a habit of fear. We think of a horse less as the history of one man and his sorrows than as the history of an entire evil age. Why I chose Never, I shall never know. I fed him odd lettuce, an abundance of bitterness. Who wore the bit and harness — who was the ready steed? Never took the carrot, and with it, words by my own reckoning: an account of creeks and oystercatchers.

Our hoof-house rested at the foot of the mountain, upon which stood another house, more brazen than statuary. Let it be known: I first mistook *gelding* for *gilding*. I am the fool who places his faith in Never. Somewhere, a gold door, burdened with apology, refuses all mint from the yard.
outputs.L2:
At the horse barn, every stall bore its occupant's name inscribed above it. Biscuit remained distant and unreachable — what I saw of him was perpetually the same: his tail swishing with mechanical regularity. Crab had grown far too familiar with the salt block. Trapezoid, meanwhile, embodied perfect motionlessness: a mare dark as midnight, the harshest and most towering of them all, her body pressing outward against the confines of her enclosure.

Never held no terror for me — this chestnut gelding whose iron flanks carried me all the way to Panther Gap. Back then, Never and I made our home in Virginia. Neither escape nor confinement suited us. Rarely did I climb that modest peak without him beside me, its gentle rises turning fields of unremarkable grass into valleys.

What was that faint noise that reached me while I sat with Never in solitude? A solitary horse becomes a guiding star, becomes an ingrained dread. We tend to regard a horse not merely as one man's personal chronicle of grief, but as testimony to an entire era's corruption.

I could never explain what drew me to choose Never. I offered him strange greens, a surplus of bitterness. Which of us truly bore the bit and harness — which one served as the willing mount? Never accepted the carrot along with my own peculiar narration, a tale spun from creek beds and shorebirds.

Our stable sat nestled at the mountain's base, above which stood a second dwelling, one more ostentatious than any sculpture. Let this be confessed: I once confused the word "gelding" with "gilding." I remain the fool who places his trust in Never. Somewhere out there, a golden door, weighted down with unspoken regret, turns away every coin the yard has to offer.
outputs.L3:
The stables held their own quiet hierarchy of temperament, and I came to know each horse the way one learns the moods of difficult relatives. Biscuit kept to himself, ears pinned back at anything resembling affection, as though friendliness were a debt he refused to incur. Crab, by contrast, had made a lifelong study of the salt lick, visiting it with the devotion of a pilgrim returning to a familiar shrine. And then there was Trapezoid—tall, dark as midnight, and possessed of a stillness that seemed less like calm than like waiting. She stood in her stall as if she were guarding something, though I never learned what.

It was Never I rode, a chestnut gelding whose name I chose without fear, though I could not always explain why. We traveled together often, out toward Panther Gap, in those years when I lived in Virginia and the land still felt unmapped to me, full of hollows and light I hadn't yet learned to name. There was no hesitation in those rides, only the steady rhythm of hooves against packed earth, the gap opening ahead of us like a door in the hills.

Looking back now, I think a horse is never only itself. It carries, without knowing it, the weight of more than one person's story—riders long gone, hands that once held these same reins, griefs and hopes folded invisibly into muscle and mane. Perhaps Never carried something larger still: not just my history, but the history of a troubled era, one I was only beginning to understand from the back of a borrowed animal in unfamiliar country.

I've never been entirely sure why I chose him, of all the horses in that stable. Something in his stillness, maybe, or the way he seemed unbothered by my inexperience. I'll admit, too, to an embarrassing confusion in those early days—I misheard "gelding" as "gilding," and for a while I imagined Never as something gilded, edged in gold, rather than simply altered, simply gentled by circumstance. The mistake seems, in retrospect, oddly fitting.

I know now that trusting him so completely was, in some sense, foolish. I knew little about horses, less about the world I was riding into, and nothing at all about what Never himself might have been thinking beneath that quiet exterior. And yet I trusted him anyway, and I still do, in memory if nowhere else. That faith remains, stubborn and unexamined, the way one keeps returning to a locked door—gold, perhaps, or only gilded—that refuses, no matter what is offered, ever to open.
outputs.L4:
# Faith in Never

I.

In Virginia, the stables smell of hay and rust and something older than both. Never stands in the third stall from the door, the one with morning light slanting through in a blade that catches his coat—not gold, never gold, though I have wanted to call it that. Gelding for gilding. The tongue slips. The eye deceives. He is not made of anything precious, only muscle and the memory of muscle, the way a body holds the shape of what it once could do.

II.

They named him Never before I knew him. A joke, maybe, or a warning. Never again. Never mind. Never say never—though someone must have said it, standing in this same doorway, watching a foal test his legs against the ungiving world. I did not choose the name. I inherited it, the way you inherit a scar or a superstition. Now I say it to call him in from the field and it means come, it means here, it means yes.

III.

Faith in Never. Say it slowly and it becomes a confession: I believe in nothing. Say it quickly and it becomes devotion: I trust this animal completely. The paradox does not resolve. It sits in the mouth like a bit, cold and necessary, shaping the shape of what can be said.

IV.

He lets me approach only if I do not look at him directly. This is not fear, exactly—or it is fear wearing the coat of ritual. I learned to walk sideways, to speak to the middle distance, to let my hand arrive before my gaze. Trust, I have come to think, is built from misdirection. We look away so the other can be seen.

V.

Memory works the same crooked way. I try to recall the first time I touched his flank and get instead the light that day, gold—no, not gold—amber, or something between amber and rust, the color of Virginia in late September when the fields go the color of his coat and I cannot tell, walking toward the stable, whether I am walking toward a horse or a held breath, a held breath or a name.

VI.

Gelding for gilding: the mistake I keep making. He is cut, altered, made gentle by absence—no wildness left to master, no seed to carry forward. And yet I gild him anyway in memory, dress him in a shine he does not wear, because faith requires a little decoration, a little lie laid gently over the surface of the true.

VII.

What does it mean to have faith in Never? Perhaps only this: that the things we love best are the things that withhold themselves, that the horse who lets me closest is the one who might, on another day, for no reason, refuse me entirely. Perhaps faith is only the willingness to keep walking toward a name that means both everything and its opposite.

VIII.

Evenings, I bring him in from the field. The light is doing its late thing, its almost-gold thing, and he comes without hurry, the way he always comes, as though arrival were a kind of forgetting. I call his name. Never. He turns his great head. And for a moment—only a moment—the word means only him: not absence, not negation, just a gelding standing in Virginia light, mistaken, as ever, for something gilded.

IX.

I have stopped trying to correct the mistake. Some misnamings are truer than the names they replace. He is Never and he is here. He is cut and he is whole. He is rust-colored and I call it gold. Faith, I have decided, is not the absence of error. It is what error becomes when you decide to keep it.

# The Trapezoid Crab Biscuit Incident

Marina had never intended to become famous for baking, but the trapezoid-shaped crab biscuits she created for the seaside café changed everything.

It started as an accident. She'd been experimenting with a savory biscuit recipe, folding in flakes of fresh crab meat, old bay seasoning, and a touch of sharp cheddar. When she went to cut the dough, her usual circular cutter was nowhere to be found. In a pinch, she grabbed a trapezoid-shaped cutter she'd bought years ago for a geometry-themed children's party and never used.

The result was unexpectedly perfect. The trapezoid shape meant that each biscuit had a wider end that crisped up beautifully, packed with more surface area for buttery, golden crust, while the narrower end stayed soft and fluffy, practically melting with crab flavor. Customers started requesting them specifically, describing the texture contrast as "genius," though Marina always laughed it off as a happy accident born of a missing cookie cutter.

Word spread through the small coastal town quickly. Local fishermen would trade their freshest catch for a dozen of her crab biscuits. A food blogger visiting from the city stumbled upon the café, tried one, and posted a rave review that read simply: "Why has no one thought of trapezoid biscuits before? The shape isn't just gimmicky, it's structurally brilliant."

Marina eventually gave in and ordered custom trapezoid cutters in bulk. She never did find her old circular one. Some mysteries, she decided, were better left unsolved, especially when the accidental replacement made for such better biscuits.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a childhood spent riding a horse named "Never" in Virginia, blending memory with wordplay.
counterfactuals.output:
# Never, in Virginia

I rode Never through the tobacco-colored dusk of childhood, her hooves striking questions into the red clay that never got answered. *Never*, my mother called across the fields, *time for supper*, and I would come, because that was always the trick of it—Never was the horse I rode, but never was also the country we lived in, a Virginia of the mind where the Blue Ridge folded up like a letter never sent.

She was seventeen hands of absence, my Never, black as the space between stars, and she ate sugar cubes from my palm like she was eating the future, one white tooth at a time. I never fell off her. That's not true. I fell constantly, into the mud, into the mountains, into the long green throat of summer, and each time she'd wait, cropping grass, patient as a word waiting to be spoken.

We galloped past the Godwin place, past the Baptist church with its steeple like an accusing finger, past Miss Hattie's clothesline where sheets swelled and sighed like ghosts practicing their lines. *Never say never*, Miss Hattie always warned, snapping wet cotton, and I never understood if she meant the horse or the word or the deep well of childhood where both things drowned together, indistinguishable, singing.

Some nights I dreamed she spoke. *I will carry you*, she said, *nowhere and back, that's my only route.* And I believed her the way children believe barns are always red, the way they believe their fathers will never die, the way tobacco leaves believe in rain.

Virginia unspooled beneath her like a green ribbon torn from something larger—the Commonwealth, the country, the century. We rode until the Piedmont turned to Tidewater turned to memory turned to this: a woman decades gone from home, still feeling phantom hoofbeats in her sternum, still hearing her mother's voice folding through screen doors—*never, never, never*—not a warning now but a name, the only horse I ever loved, the only word for what childhood does to time: it gallops. It does not arrive. It never, ever arrives, and yet here I am, still riding, still called home through the dusk that has no bottom, on the back of a horse that was never mine to keep, in a Virginia that was never quite the world, only its rehearsal, green and endless and gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental flash fiction centered on stable stalls, horse names, and a pun on "gelding" and "gilding."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Gilded Gelding

Stall seven held a horse named Midas, which everyone agreed was either too obvious or exactly obvious enough.

*

The stable smelled of hay and ammonia and something older—the accumulated breath of animals who had learned patience the hard way. Marguerite walked the aisle each morning counting names like rosary beads: Whisper, Thunderclap, Judge Not, Loose Change.

*

They gelded him in October, when the leaves were doing their annual impression of currency.

*

*Gelding*, the vet said. *Standard procedure.*

*Gilding*, Marguerite heard, because she was tired, because the barn light caught dust motes like suspended flecks of gold, because language is a horse that sometimes throws its rider.

*

Stall seven, empty for three days of recovery. The nameplate still read MIDAS. She touched the brass letters—actual gilt, actually gold-leafed by some previous owner with more sentiment than sense—and thought about the difference between adding value and removing it. Between what you put on a thing and what you take away.

*

The other horses in their stalls: Six, Nine, Twelve. Numbers where names should be, the way some thoughts arrive as blanks where words should be.

*

*He'll be calmer now,* the vet said. *Easier to handle.*

*He'll be less himself now,* Marguerite thought, and didn't say, because there's no vet for that kind of subtraction.

*

When Midas returned to stall seven, he moved like something unburdened. Or diminished. The barn light still gilded everything it touched—his coat, the hay dust, the brass letters spelling out a name that had outlived its own accuracy.

*

Gold doesn't care what it's covering. That's the thing about gilding—it sits on top, indifferent to what's underneath, whether myth or muscle or the quiet architecture of what used to make a stallion a stallion.

*

Marguerite fed him an apple. He accepted it the way he accepted everything now: without the old electric wariness, without the coiled particular *thereness* that had made him Midas instead of Six or Nine or Twelve.

*

Still gold, though. Still gold on the outside.

*

That's what she couldn't stop thinking, walking the aisle at dusk, past all the stalls with their brass nameplates catching the same dying light: we gild what we've gelded. We shine up what we've simplified. We call it *calm* and mean *quieter*. We call it *manageable* and mean *made smaller*.

*

The horse named Midas stood in his stall, gold-adjacent, touching nothing that turned to treasure anymore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, fragmented narrative about horses in a stable, where each horse's name carries symbolic weight, ending with an image of a gold door.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Stable at the Edge of Sleep

They keep horses here, or the memory of horses—
manes like unraveling rope, breath fogging
the cold iron air.

**Sorrow** stands in the third stall, hoof-worn and patient.
She does not toss her head. She has learned
that grief, too, needs feeding twice a day,
needs someone to check her water.

*Down the row—*

**Ash** who was once called something else,
something with fire in it, before the barn
half-burned and they renamed him
for what remained.

**Quiet** paces. Quiet is the loudest one,
kicking the boards at 3 a.m.,
as if silence were a thing
you could wear thin.

*Names are not descriptions. Names are wounds
we agreed to call by gentler words.*

**Marrow** leans into the wall, old bones singing
under old skin. When they say *good boy*
they mean *thank you for staying
inside your body this long.*

**Little Mercy**, the newest, still learning
the weight of her own legs,
does not yet know
what she was named for surviving.

*The stable smells of hay and rust and something
underneath that—copper, or memory,
or the ghost of every hand
that ever came here open.*

At the end of the row, past all the names
that mean more than horses,
past Sorrow's slow blink
and Ash's flinch at matches
and Quiet's terrible noise—

there is a door.

Not wood. Not iron.
Gold, though no one painted it that color,
gold like something earned,
gold like the last good field
before the field ends—

and it is closed,

and it is warm to the touch,

and none of them, not one,
has ever tried to open it,
as if some doors are meant
only to be walked toward,
slowly,
in the dark,
by animals who have already
survived their names.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic short story exploring themes of naming, memory, and fear through the relationship between a narrator and a horse called Never.
counterfactuals.output:
# What We Call the Things We Love

The horse came without a name, the way all terrible, beautiful things do. My grandfather found him in the flooded bottomland, ribs like fence slats, eyes rolling white at the sky as if the sky had personally wronged him. Some animals arrive already grieving something they cannot name. This was one of those.

"What will you call him?" I asked, seven years old and full of the confidence of naming things—stones, clouds, the particular ache behind my breastbone I would later learn was called *longing*.

My grandfather considered the horse the way he considered scripture, weather, and his own approaching death: slowly, and without flinching.

"Never," he said.

"Never what?"

"Just Never."

I did not understand then that some names are not labels but warnings. That to call something Never is to press your palm against a wound and say *here, this is where it hurts, remember this.*

---

Never grew into his name the way children grow into their fathers' faces—unwillingly, inevitably. He would not be caught in open pasture. He would not cross the creek at the low ford though every other horse did. He flinched from open doorways, from the particular blue of my grandfather's oldest coat, from the sound of certain bells.

"He remembers something," my grandfather said, "that his body knows and his mind has lost."

I used to sit on the fence and study Never's face, looking for the shape of whatever had hollowed him out. I thought if I understood his fear, I could rename it—could call it *thunder* or *rope* or *fire* and thereby make it small enough to hold. But fear that has no name is not fear that has been forgotten. It is fear that has become the animal itself. You cannot separate the horse from the haunting. You cannot separate the wound from the walking wound.

---

I am older now than my grandfather was when he found Never in the flood-mud. I have my own doorways I will not walk through, my own blue coats, my own bells that ring some old alarm in a body that has outlived its reasons.

I think of Never in the mornings sometimes, how he'd stand at the far corner of the pasture, watching the gate like it might open on its own and swallow him. How my grandfather would walk out slow, no rope, no bridle, just his open hands and his low voice saying *nothing's coming, nothing's coming*—

Which was, of course, a kind of lie. Something was always coming. That's what Never knew, in the wordless country of his animal grief, that the rest of us spend our lives trying to forget: everything comes eventually. The flood. The rope. The last blue coat folded into a box.

We name our fears to make them small, to make them stories we can walk around. But some names are not cages. Some names are just the truth, said plainly, so that when it finally arrives—

when the water rises, when the gate swings open, when the thing we have spent our whole lives flinching from finally, finally reveals its face—

we are not surprised.

We simply nod, the way Never nodded, the way my grandfather nodded, the way I am learning, slowly, to nod.

*Ah. There you are. I have been calling you by name since before I knew your face.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract, dreamlike prose piece using horse imagery and stable life to meditate on faith, history, and the passage of time.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Stable

There is a horse in the dark that has been running since before your grandmother's grandmother learned her name. You do not see it. You feel it—the drum of it beneath the floorboards, beneath the frost-hard field, beneath the bones of things that used to have names and now are only weight in the ground.

The stable stands at the edge of what you know. Beams silvered gray as unspoken prayer. Someone built it once, hammer-struck and hopeful, believing shelter was a kind of promise you could keep. And maybe it was. The roof still holds, though the rain finds its way in like doubt finds its way into any faith worth having.

Inside: the smell of hay and ammonia and something older, something like memory fermenting in the corners. Each stall a small chapel. Each nail a genuflection.

You come here not to ride but to listen.

The horses breathe in the darkness—not one horse now but many, layered like sediment, like scripture written over scripture until the original words are only a pressure beneath the new ones. A bay mare who carried a farmer's son to war. A gray gelding who pulled the plow through seasons that don't have names anymore. Foals born and buried in the same afternoon, their small shapes dissolving into the field's slow green forgetting.

Time moves here the way a horse moves in sleep—standing, always standing, legs locked in that ancient animal trust that the ground will hold, that morning will come, that the weight of being alive is bearable if you do not think too hard about gravity.

Faith is this: leaning your whole weight against a door and believing it will open.

Faith is: the bridle you cannot see, guiding you anyway.

Somewhere a bell that no one rings still marks the hour. The horse keeps running. The stable keeps standing. You keep listening in the dark for hoofbeats that might be your own pulse, might be the pulse of everyone who stood here before you, ear pressed to the wood, waiting to be told something true.

The dust motes fall like scripture pages.
The horse does not stop.
You were never meant to catch it—
only to hear it pass,
and call that passing *God*,
and call that hearing *home*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
